title: How to Manage Subliminator Variants Without Bloating Your Catalog
excerpt: A catalog discipline guide for all-over print sellers: how to decide which cuts, colorways, and sizes deserve a variant, how to version artwork files, and when to delist.
body: All-over print makes it tempting to publish every colorway of every cut, because the marginal cost of one more variant looks like zero. It is not zero. Each variant adds a mockup to maintain, a page element to load, and one more chance for a customer to land on a size that is out of stock. Catalog bloat is the quiet reason print-on-demand stores lose conversion rate as they grow. The fix is not fewer products, it is a deliberate rule about which variants exist.

Start with the cut, then the print, then the size. Decide which garment cuts you will carry for a given design and hold that list fixed for a season. Within each cut, limit colorways to the two or three that actually sell, which you learn from your own order data rather than from what the supplier offers. Size runs should follow the same logic, and extended sizes should be a conscious choice with its own cost check, not a default toggle that expands every listing at once.

Version your artwork files the same way you version code. A sublimation print sits on a specific cut at a specific bleed, so a design approved on a tee is not automatically correct on a hoodie or a legging. Keep one master file per design and one production file per cut, named with the design and the cut. When you update artwork, update every dependent file in the same session. Most visual defects in made-to-order apparel trace back to a file that was updated in one place and not another.

Set a stock and delisting rule before the catalog grows. If a variant has no orders in ninety days and no traffic in thirty, pull it. If a size is chronically unavailable, hide it rather than showing an option that fails at checkout. Re-run this pass quarterly, and keep a simple sheet of what was removed and why, because suppliers reintroduce colors and you will want to know which ones you already tested. A smaller catalog with accurate availability converts better than a large one full of dead ends.

Watch the metrics that reveal bloat. Track the share of product page views that land on variants with zero sales, the average number of variants a shopper scrolls before abandoning, and the number of support tickets that start with a size or color question. Those three numbers tell you whether the catalog is helping or hurting. If the zero-sales share is above a third of your views, the next useful move is subtraction, not another launch.

Then fold the survivors into your merchandising. Group the cuts that share a design into one product page where the platform allows it, and let the best-selling colorway lead the gallery. The DTCwise Subliminator listing at /tool/subliminator covers product range and file requirements, and the Print-on-Demand category at /category/pod keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing.
